title: When not to mock
description: Learn which React patterns and dependencies should never be mocked, how to trust your tests more by mocking less, and the heuristics senior engineers use to decide.

data.text: Mocking is a powerful tool, but over-mocking is the single biggest cause of test suites that pass in CI but break in production. A senior frontend engineer knows that the goal of a test is to catch real bugs, and the more you replace with mocks, the less real-world behavior your tests cover.

This lesson focuses on the inverse question: when should you leave the real implementation in place? The answer depends on three factors — the cost of running the real code, the volatility of the code under test, and the risk if the integration silently breaks.
Things you should almost never mock

items: Your UI framework: never mock React itself. If React breaks, you want your tests to fail, not silently pass.
Routing: React Router and similar libraries are stable, well-tested upstream, and cheap to render.
State management libraries you do not own: Redux, Zustand, and Jotai work fine in tests and catch selector bugs.
Utility functions: pure functions like date formatters, string helpers, or validation schemas should be tested directly, not via mocks.
Custom hooks that do not touch the network: hooks like useDebounce, useLocalStorage, or useMediaQuery are cheap and deterministic.

data.text: A concrete example: do not mock useForm
A common mistake is mocking a form hook and then asserting on the mock's internal state. Here is why that approach breaks down, followed by the better alternative:

data.caption: Bad: mocking useForm hides real validation behavior
Good: let the real hook run and interact with it through the DOM

data.text: The second test uses the real hook and the real validation logic. It catches the same bug a user would hit in production.

items: If the real code is slower than 100 ms and deterministic, leave it real.
If the real code depends on network or filesystem, replace it with a fake or stub — never a full mock of the interface.
If you find yourself re-creating the real behavior in a mock body, you are mocking too much.
If a test fails only because the mock was not updated after a refactor, the mock is the problem, not the test.

data.title: Mock-only-what-you-own principle
data.text: As a rough rule, avoid mocking code you do not control. Third-party libraries have their own test suites. Your job is to verify that your code integrates with them correctly, not to recreate their behavior in mock return values.

items: Network calls: Replace with MSW interceptors or a stub, not a hand-written mock object.
Timers: Use fake timers (vi.useFakeTimers()) for debounce and throttle logic.
Browser APIs not available in jsdom: IntersectionObserver, matchMedia, ResizeObserver.
Expensive computation: A slow image processing function that takes seconds should be stubbed in unit tests, but also tested in a separate slow integration suite.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Mocking the real implementation is a trade-off, not a default.
Leave React, routing, state libraries, and pure utilities unmocked.
Replace only slow, non-deterministic, or external dependencies.
A test that mocks everything tests nothing.
